chapters.title: Chapter 2: Economic Terms an Angel Must Negotiate

lessons.title: Anti-Dilution and Pro-Rata Clauses: How They Actually Read in a Term Sheet

children.text: The prerequisite cap tables course already taught the idea behind full ratchet and weighted average anti-dilution, and when pro-rata rights are worth defending. What it did not show is the actual formula a term sheet writes down, or the actual clause language that decides whether Rohan gets to use his pro-rata right at all. This lesson closes that gap, using the conversion ratio mechanism from the previous lesson.

body.text: Anti-dilution protection is not a vague promise. It is a formula, applied to the conversion price, that a term sheet writes down in exact terms. Read the formula, and you can compute precisely how many extra equity shares a down round hands you, before it ever happens.

children.text: Broad-based weighted average, the market standard for Indian angel and Series A rounds, adjusts the conversion price using this formula.

body.caption: CP1 is the conversion price before the down round. CP2 is the adjusted conversion price after it.

children.text: A, B and C are all share counts. A is the shares outstanding immediately before the down round, on a fully diluted basis. B is the number of shares the new money would have bought at the old, higher conversion price. C is the number of shares the new money actually buys, at the new, lower price. A bigger gap between B and C, meaning a steeper price drop, pulls CP2 down further and gives Rohan a bigger conversion ratio.

"Clause 27, Anti-Dilution Protection (illustrative wording): In the event the Company issues Equity Securities at a price per share lower than the Conversion Price then in effect for the CCPS (a 'Down Round'), the Conversion Price of the CCPS shall be adjusted on a broad-based weighted average basis in accordance with the formula set out in Schedule C, calculated on a fully diluted basis including the Company's employee stock option pool, whether or not allocated."
Suppose ChaiCart later raises ₹40,00,000 in a down round at ₹1,600 per share, exactly half of the ₹3,200 Rohan paid in the Series A.

stats.label: A: shares outstanding before
stats.context: Fully diluted, before the down round

stats.label: B: shares at the old price

children.text: CP2 = ₹3,200 × (15,625 + 1,250) ÷ (15,625 + 2,500) = ₹3,200 × 16,875 ÷ 18,125 ≈ ₹2,979.31. Rohan's new conversion ratio is ₹3,200 ÷ ₹2,979.31 ≈ 1.074, so his 625 CCPS would now convert into roughly 671 equity shares instead of 625, a real cap table tool would carry more decimal precision, but the shape of the adjustment is clear: a meaningful cushion, not a dramatic one.
How Much Worse Is Full Ratchet

Full ratchet ignores B and C entirely. It simply resets the conversion price straight to the new round's price, however small that round was. Here, CP2 becomes ₹1,600 outright, giving a conversion ratio of ₹3,200 ÷ ₹1,600 = 2.0 exactly. Rohan's 625 CCPS would convert into 1,250 equity shares, exactly double, regardless of whether ChaiCart raised ₹40,00,000 or just ₹4,00,000 in that round.

body.title: Rohan's equity shares on conversion, by anti-dilution structure

body.label: Full ratchet is rare in Indian early-stage deals
body.value: Broad-based weighted average is the market standard
body.context: Full ratchet is considered aggressively investor-friendly and shows up mostly in distressed financings or unusually one-sided rounds. Broad-based weighted average is close to universal in standard Indian angel, seed and Series A term sheets, with narrow-based sitting in between the two.

children.text: Broad-Based vs Narrow-Based: The Denominator Fight

Clause 27 specifies that A includes ChaiCart's entire ESOP pool, allocated or not. That single phrase is the whole broad-based versus narrow-based debate. A broad-based formula stuffs every possible share into A, including options nobody has been granted yet, which makes A bigger, which makes the adjustment smaller. A narrow-based formula excludes the unallocated pool, shrinking A and producing a steeper drop in CP2 for the exact same down round.

body.title: Reading the Denominator
body.question: Which version of the weighted-average formula gives ChaiCart's founders more protection from a large conversion price adjustment?
options: Broad-based, including the full option pool whether allocated or not
Narrow-based, excluding the unallocated option pool
It depends only on the size of the down round, not the formula chosen
body.explanation: A larger A, which is what a broad-based formula produces by counting the entire option pool, dampens the size of the adjustment. Narrow-based, with a smaller A, produces a steeper price drop and a bigger conversion ratio, which favours the investor over the founders.

children.text: Pro-Rata Rights: How the Clause Actually Works
A pro-rata right is usually restricted to a

, a defined threshold in the shareholders' agreement, commonly a minimum investment amount such as ₹10 lakh or more. A small enough angel cheque may not qualify for pro-rata rights at all, whatever the term sheet's headline terms say about follow-on investment.

markDefs.definition: A defined threshold, usually a minimum investment amount, that an investor must clear to receive certain contractual rights such as pro-rata participation and information rights.

children.text: "Clause 31, Pro-Rata Right (illustrative wording): Prior to issuing any new Equity Securities other than Exempted Securities, the Company shall first offer each Major Investor the right to purchase its Pro-Rata Share of such new Equity Securities, on the same price and terms offered to the proposed purchaser, by written notice specifying the terms of the proposed issuance. Each Major Investor shall have 15 (fifteen) Business Days from receipt of such notice to elect, in writing, to purchase all or part of its Pro-Rata Share, failing which the right shall lapse solely in respect of that issuance."

body.caption: "Exempted Securities": issuances that do not trigger the pro-rata right

cells: Shares or options issued under an approved ESOP plan
A normal part of compensating employees, not a fundraising event
Shares issued as consideration in a merger or acquisition
Not a cash fundraise the investor could meaningfully participate in
Shares issued on conversion of existing CCPS or CCDs
Already accounted for when those instruments were first issued
No new money changes hands, so there is nothing to buy into
Shares issued to an approved strategic partner or lender, up to an agreed cap
A negotiated exception for non-financial investors the company wants flexibility to bring in

body.title: The Oversubscribed Round
body.scenario: Rohan qualifies as a Major Investor under ChaiCart's SHA. ChaiCart's Series B is heavily oversubscribed, and Ananya asks Rohan informally to accept a smaller allocation than his full pro-rata share so a strategic investor can get more room.
body.prompt: Is ChaiCart within its rights to scale back Rohan's allocation like this?
body.modelAnswer: Not unilaterally. Clause 31 gives every Major Investor the right to purchase its full pro-rata share once written notice is given, and oversubscription by other investors does not override that right unless Rohan agrees to accept less. Ananya can ask, and plenty of angels accommodate a founder's request to make room for a strategic investor, especially when the relationship matters more than the extra allocation, but she cannot force a scale-back on her own. Rohan's real decision here is commercial rather than legal: whether preserving goodwill with ChaiCart is worth voluntarily giving up part of a right he could otherwise enforce.

body.title: What Doesn't Trigger the Right
body.question: Which of the following would NOT trigger Rohan's pro-rata right under Clause 31?
options: A ₹2 crore Series B round sold to a new external investor
A fresh grant of stock options to a new engineering hire under ChaiCart's approved ESOP plan
A private placement of new CCPS to a new angel investor
A follow-on round where ChaiCart sells additional CCPS to fund expansion
body.explanation: ESOP grants under an approved plan are a standard Exempted Security. Every other option here is a genuine issuance of new equity securities for cash to a third party, exactly what a pro-rata right is designed to let a Major Investor participate in.

body.title: Anti-Dilution and Pro-Rata, in Clause Form

cards.definition: A is fully diluted shares outstanding before the down round. B is shares the new money would buy at the old price. C is shares actually issued at the new, lower price.
A weighted-average formula where A includes the entire option pool, allocated or not, producing a smaller, more founder-friendly adjustment.
A weighted-average formula that excludes the unallocated option pool from A, producing a steeper, more investor-friendly adjustment.
An anti-dilution structure that resets the conversion price straight to the new round's price, regardless of how many shares were actually issued.
A defined investment threshold an investor must clear to receive rights such as pro-rata participation and information rights.
Issuances, such as ESOP grants or M&A consideration shares, that are carved out from triggering a pro-rata right.

points: Broad-based weighted average anti-dilution is a specific formula, CP2 = CP1 × (A+B)/(A+C), not just a general idea, and it can be computed before a down round even happens.
Whether A includes the unallocated ESOP pool (broad-based) or excludes it (narrow-based) changes how severe the adjustment is, even for the identical down round.
Full ratchet ignores the size of the down round entirely and simply resets the conversion price to the new round's price, producing a far larger adjustment than weighted average.
Broad-based weighted average is the market standard in Indian angel and Series A rounds. Full ratchet is rare and generally signals a distressed or unusually investor-favourable deal.
Pro-rata rights are usually gated behind a Major Investor threshold, so a small enough cheque may not qualify for them at all.

A pro-rata clause lists specific Exempted Securities, such as ESOP grants and M&A shares, that do not trigger the right, and gives the investor a fixed notice period to exercise it before it lapses for that issuance.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal or investment advice. ChaiCart, Rohan and Ananya are fictional and used for illustration, and the clause language, formula inputs and figures shown are illustrative rather than a template for a real transaction. Anti-dilution and pro-rata mechanics vary significantly by deal and should be reviewed by a qualified lawyer before you rely on them. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid, and can result in the loss of your entire capital.
